rashi:a1.1: Concerning ritual impurity, what does Rabbi Yehuda say: does he hold that there is a full term [melot] for the second [offspring] with regard to the days of purity?
rashi:a1.2: Rabbi Yehuda says it only with regard to the offering: it is there that he holds that the second has no full term, since it was born within the time of the first one’s offering.
rashi:a1.3: But with regard to impurity and purity: she counts for it [the second] on its own, apart from those [days] of the first; the days of impurity are called by its name and are taken out of the term of the first.
rashi:a1.4: And the impurity of the second interrupts: the days of purity of the first, and she completes the days of purity of the first, since according to Rabbi Yehuda it is impossible not to complete the term of the first, for it is the principal one; and then she counts eighty days, days of purity, for the second.
rashi:a2.1: Or perhaps he holds a stringency: to increase the offerings; and he assigns days of impurity and days of purity to the second from the time of its birth onward, and she is barred from eating sacrificial food until the days of impurity and purity are complete. But a leniency he does not hold: that the days of impurity be called by the name of the second so that she completes [the term] of the first in their place. For in this matter, too, it is as though it does not exist, and we do not complete the days of purity of the first and then complete other days of purity for the second in their place, since that is a leniency, prolonging the purity of her blood [the period in which blood she sees is pure], and a leniency he does not hold. And one cannot say that the second is entirely void of the law of a term, for that too is a leniency: if so, she would be fit to eat sacrificial food as one who immersed that day [tevulat yom]. Perforce you must assign days of purity to the second. Therefore, if you give the first the completion of its days of purity, it is a leniency.
rashi:a3.1: One slaughters: the Paschal offering, and sprinkles [its blood] on her account on the fortieth day for a male. [The Gemara] initially assumes: on the fortieth day of the days of purity of a male.
rashi:a4.1: And we discussed it: until now she is impure: since she is lacking atonement.
rashi:a4.2: Rav Ḥisda said: Whose is this? It is Rabbi Yehuda, who says the second offspring is as though it does not exist: and he establishes this baraita as dealing with a woman who gave birth to twins, one today and the second tomorrow, so that the fortieth day of the second is the forty-first of the first, and today she is fit to bring her offering for the first. And it teaches us that one slaughters on her account even though she is lacking atonement, and after her Paschal offering is slaughtered she brings her atonement offering and eats of her Paschal offering in the evening. Evidently the second offspring is as though it does not exist, so that it does not hold her back by requiring her to count for it, which would extend her days of purity until the next day.
rashi:a5.1: And if you say that concerning impurity Rabbi Yehuda holds that it is as though it exists: so that its days of impurity cause a completion of the days of purity of the first; how does one slaughter? In the evening, too, she could not eat it, for the second offspring caused the days of purity of the first to be extended by one day: the eighth day of the first is the seventh of the second and is one of its days of impurity, so it interrupted the count of the first, and she must complete it; and until day forty-two of the first she is not fit to bring her atonement offering. Rather, must one not conclude from it that it is as though it does not exist, and its days of impurity and purity count toward the tally of the days of purity of the first?
rashi:a6.1: Actually, I could say to you, etc.: and that baraita is not established as dealing with a second offspring but with any ordinary birth. And as for your difficulty that in the evening, too, she is lacking atonement: we are dealing with a Paschal offering brought in impurity, where most of the community became impure, and impurity was permitted for her.
rashi:a7.1: May not partake of it, etc.: for when impurity is permitted for the community, it is permitted with regard to impurity imparted by a corpse, as it is written: “If any man shall be impure by reason of a corpse” (Numbers 9:10), and on this we expound (Pesaḥim 66b): An individual is deferred to the second Pesaḥ, but a community is not deferred; rather, they perform it in impurity.
rashi:a8.1: They do not partake when they did not immerse: [men and women] whose discharge had not ceased, or had ceased but who had not counted seven [clean days] and had not immersed. But a woman after childbirth, on the fortieth day, had immersed on the eighth day after her birth.
rashi:a8.2: If that is so: why does it mention the fortieth day for a male or the eightieth for a female? From the eighth day after her birth she is also fit.
rashi:a10.1: On the fortieth day she is also not fit: even in the evening, since she is lacking atonement. And at this point it is assumed that a zav who is lacking atonement is considered a zav and does not eat of a Paschal offering brought in impurity.
rashi:a11.1: This statement of Rava is in [tractate] Sheḥitat Kodashim [Zevaḥim], at the beginning of the second chapter (17b).
rashi:a11.2: Rav Ashi said: Rava does not resolve it as the fortieth day of the days of purity at all. Rather, he establishes it as a woman who gave birth on the fortieth day of her pregnancy and bore a male: one slaughters on her account on that very day. And it is Rabbi Yishmael, who says in the chapter HaMappelet Ḥatikha (Niddah 30a): The formation of a female is on the eighty-first day.
rashi:a12.2: The “grave” [hakever]: the womb. [The Aramaic says “the opening of the grave”; the Davidson renders it “the womb.”]
rashi:a13.1: One might have thought: whether continuous: for example, where she did not miscarry in the meantime.
rashi:a13.2: Or dispersed: for example, if she miscarried at the end of fifty-four [days], one might have thought that the impurity of the miscarriage interrupts for her, and they complete for her sixty days of purity for the first birth, apart from the days of impurity of the miscarriage that interrupt in between.
rashi:a13.3: The verse states “day”: just as a day is entirely continuous, if impure, impure, and if pure, pure, so too the sixty days are all continuous for purity.
rashi:a13.4: Do they hold of dispersed days? But she counts from the second offspring, and they do not complete the days of purity of the first; rather, they follow the last one. Therefore, according to them, you never find dispersed days.
rashi:a14.1: Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda: who holds that there are days of purity for the first, since according to him the first is the principal one with regard to the offering. And it teaches us here that with regard to impurity and purity he does not hold that there are [completed] days of purity for the first, for if so you would not find continuous days of purity for her; rather, she counts from the second. And conclude from it that he merely holds a stringency in the mishna, to increase offerings, and only with regard to the offering does she count for the first; but with regard to impurity, completing the days of purity of the first by counting them dispersed, he does not hold this, since it is a leniency, as she would again need to assign days of purity to the second.
rashi:a15.1: Actually, it is the Rabbis: and this is how you find dispersed days: a woman who gave birth to a male within the eighty [days] of a female, where the days of purity of the male end before the eighty of the first female. In a case like this, where the days of purity of the second end before the days of purity of the first, the Rabbis do not hold that she counts from the second offspring, and she must complete the days of purity of the first. And the verse comes to teach us that she does not complete, after the eighty of the first birth, seven [days] corresponding to the seven days of impurity of the male that interrupted in between; rather, she counts from the second.
rashi:a16.1: Ultimately: you do not find such a case, that the eighty of the first female are complete while the forty of the male are not yet complete, for you cannot find the birth of a male before [day] fifty-four of the female: fourteen of the female’s impurity and forty for the formation of the male. And since … [a few words here are in parentheses in the printed text and are unclear] … you do not find dispersed days.
rashi:a16.2: With a woman who gives birth to twins: who were conceived [together].
rashi:a16.3: On the twentieth of the days of purity: twenty is not precise; the same applies to fewer than this or more than this.
rashi:a17.1: Dispersed: that is, that the seven days of impurity of the male interrupted the days of purity of the female, and we would give her seven others after the eighty of the first birth. The verse states “day.”
rashi:a18.1: The thirty of a male, dispersed: for example, a woman who gave birth to twins and bore the second within the thirty of the first, a male. One might have thought that they give her seven [days] beyond the forty of the first birth, corresponding to the seven days of impurity of the second, so that now the thirty are dispersed, since the days of impurity interrupted in between and did not count toward the tally.
tosafot:a2.1: In brief: Rashi explains that the leniency Rabbi Yehuda does not hold is completing the first one’s days of purity in place of the second one’s days of impurity, and that the second is not entirely void either, since that too would be a leniency letting her eat sacrificial food, so days of purity must be given to the second. Tosafot find this unlikely. First, the Gemara brings “one slaughters and sprinkles” to prove that the second offspring is as though it does not exist; if days of purity are given to the second, why slaughter on day forty of the second, when she is still one who immersed that day and cannot bring her birth offering until the next day, day forty-one of the second? Second, on Rashi’s reading the stringency regarding sacrificial food leads to a leniency, since it permits her to her husband all those days even though she sees blood. Therefore it appears that according to Rabbi Yehuda the second is given no days of purity at all. According to the Rabbis, where the second one’s days of purity extend past the first one’s, she counts from the second, and where they do not, she counts from the first: although they hold that she counts from the second, they concede that where the first one’s days extend further, she counts from it. This is implied below, where the Gemara explains the baraita of sixty continuous days according to the Rabbis with a female first and a male born on the twentieth of the days of purity. For the Rabbis, days of impurity and days of purity are alike: she counts from the last one when its count extends beyond the other, as the Tosefta teaches that a woman after childbirth counts from the last, like one impure from a corpse who counts from the last impurity, and not like a menstruating woman, who counts from the first. Hence, if she saw blood within the seven days of her birth, it is not treated as seeing within her days of menstruation, counted from the first; she counts seven days from the sighting. And if she gave birth within her days of menstruation, she counts from the day of birth. The rule that for one offspring after another she counts from the last applies where the days of impurity of the last extend beyond those of the first, like the impurity of a zav and of a menstruating woman cited in the Tosefta. But if she bore a male four or five days after a female, we do not say that the female’s count is void and that she counts only seven days from the male, ending on day eleven or twelve of the female with days of purity beginning there; since the male’s seven days of impurity are absorbed within the female’s two weeks, the female’s days of impurity are not void. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a11.1: On the fortieth day of the formation of a male: even though one cannot know the fortieth day of formation, since semen sometimes takes up to three days to be absorbed. But Shmuel was expert in this, as we say in the chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 25b): Shmuel is different, as his ability was great.
tosafot:a12.1: It is impossible for the womb to open without blood: This is puzzling: if so, why was it necessary to write regarding a male, “and she shall be impure seven days”? And Rabbi [our teacher] says: if not for the verse, I would have said that she is impure for two weeks, by an a fortiori inference from a female: if for a female, whose purification is great, it is still two weeks, all the more so for a male, whose [purification] is small. And there is something similar in the Torat Kohanim.
tosafot:a12.2: It teaches us: that is, it is possible for the womb to open without blood. And so it is ruled in the She’iltot of Rav Aḥai, on the basis of this passage, from “one slaughters and sprinkles.”
tosafot:a14.1: Conclude from it a stringency, etc.: for one cannot say that “continuous” is like the days of counting of a zav, that no impurity may interrupt between them, so that here, too, the thirty-three days would have to be clean [of blood], since it is written: “She shall continue in the blood of purification”; evidently they need not be clean.
gershom:a1.1: [The printed text opens with an editor’s marker: “up to here belongs to 9b.”] Concerning impurity and purity: with regard to days of impurity and days of purity, how does Rabbi Yehuda regard the second offspring?
gershom:a2.1: For the time fit to bring the offering of the first had not passed before she miscarried the second; rather, she miscarried it within the term [of the first].
gershom:a3.1: And the days of impurity of the second interrupt the days of purity of the first. When the days of impurity of the second are complete, she completes the days of purity of the first, adding days of purity corresponding to those days of impurity of the second that fell within the days of purity of the first, and afterward she counts days of purity for the second. And this is a leniency, for the first loses nothing of its days of purity even though the days of impurity of the second fell within them.
gershom:a4.1: Or perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds a stringency: he is more stringent than the Rabbis, for according to the Rabbis she brings an offering only for the last, while according to Rabbi Yehuda she brings one for the first and for the third. And since he is stringent regarding the offering, he is stringent also regarding impurity and purity, so that we do not repay the first with days of purity corresponding to the days of impurity of the second; rather, the days of impurity of the second do not interrupt but count toward the tally of the days of purity of the first, for we say that with regard to impurity the second offspring is as though it does not exist.
gershom:a5.1: A woman after childbirth: one slaughters her Paschal offering and sprinkles its blood on her account on the fortieth day for a male and on the eightieth day for a female. … [A few words here are marked by the printer as unintelligible.] And it is difficult for us: on the fortieth day for a male and on the eightieth day for a female, how does one slaughter on her account? Until now she is impure with regard to the offering, since the time fit to bring the offering has not yet come, as she brings the offering only on day forty-one or eighty-one.
gershom:a6.1: And Rav Ḥisda said: this baraita is to be explained, and it is like this: for example, where she gave birth to twins on two [consecutive] days, and when it teaches “on the fortieth day for a male,” it means the fortieth day of the second male, which is day forty-one of the first male, and day eighty-one of the first female. And it is Rabbi Yehuda, who says the second offspring is as though it does not exist, and it is already day forty-one; therefore one slaughters on her account. For if you say that concerning impurity Rabbi Yehuda holds, etc.
gershom:a7.1: In the evening, too: on the night of [day] eighty-one, which is the night of Pesaḥ, she could not eat it, for even though she brings the offering the next day, at night she is still short of the time for her offering, and she is lacking atonement. Rather, must one not conclude, etc.
gershom:a8.1: Actually: he holds that it is as though it exists. [And as for your difficulty] why one slaughters on her account: when that baraita is taught, that one slaughters on her account, it is about a Paschal offering brought in impurity, where most of the community were impure from corpses and performed it in impurity; and since it is brought in impurity, she can eat of it.
gershom:a9.1: And does she partake of it? But didn’t we learn: zavim, zavot, menstruating women and women after childbirth may not partake of it; for it is eaten in impurity only by a community impure from corpses.
gershom:a10.1: When it teaches that zavim, zavot, menstruating women and women after childbirth may not partake of it, [it means] that they do not eat in their days of impurity when they have not yet immersed. And when it teaches that one slaughters on her account on the fortieth day, it is because she has already immersed.
gershom:a11.1: If so: that immersion is effective, then from her eighth day, when she immersed, she is fit for one to slaughter on her account; why does it mention the fortieth day, [if the reason is] that she had already immersed? [It answers:] for a male, not from the eighth: until the fortieth she is not fit for one to slaughter on her account, since it holds that a zav who immersed that day is considered a full zav, so that one cannot slaughter on his account until his sun has set. Here, too, a woman after childbirth who immersed that day is like a woman after childbirth: from the eighth until the fortieth day is like one long day, and this is the “long tevul yom” mentioned in tractate Niddah. And sunset is not considered [to have come] for her until the evening of the fortieth day.
gershom:a12.1: If so, on the fortieth day she is also not fit to eat in the evening, since she is lacking atonement.
gershom:a13.1: No, on the fortieth day she is fit: in the evening, since it holds that a zav lacking atonement is not considered a zav, and one can slaughter on his account; so too a woman after childbirth lacking atonement.
gershom:a14.1: And according to Rava, who says in tractate Zevaḥim that a zav lacking atonement is considered a zav, how does he resolve “on the fortieth day for a male”?
gershom:a15.1: Rava resolves it: one slaughters on her account on the fortieth day of the formation of a male. That is, if, from the day she immersed and conceived, she miscarried on the fortieth day, when there is concern about the formation of a male: had she miscarried the next day, on day forty-one, and it was a male, its form would be recognizable, according to Rabbi Yishmael, who says a male is complete on day forty-one and a female on day eighty-one. Now, since she miscarried one day before its form was complete, it is not considered an offspring. Therefore one slaughters on her account when she miscarried on the fortieth day of the formation of a male or on the eightieth of the formation of a female.
gershom:a16.1: Ultimately: why does one slaughter on her account when she miscarried on day forty? Let me derive [that one does not], since one does not slaughter [on her account] in impurity because she is menstruating, as every woman after childbirth is a menstruating woman.
gershom:a17.1: In a dry birth: in which there was no blood at all.
gershom:a18.1: If so, that there is no blood, it is obvious that one slaughters [on her account].
gershom:a19.1: Lest you say it is impossible for the womb to open without blood: and she saw blood and it was lost.
gershom:a20.1: It teaches us that it is possible for the womb to open without blood.
gershom:a21.1: One might have thought: whether continuous: all sixty without interruption, and that is a stringency. For example, she gave birth to a female and then miscarried again within the days of purity of the first, so that the days of impurity of the second fell within the days of purity of the first. If we say that we need sixty continuous days, the days of impurity of the second count toward the sixty and are taken off the days of purity of the first.
gershom:a22.1: Or one might have thought, sixty whether dispersed: that is a leniency, that is, the days of impurity of the second interrupt the days of purity of the first, and afterward they complete the days of purity of the first after the days of impurity of the second, and she loses nothing of her days of purity.
gershom:a23.1: The verse states “day”: just as a day is entirely continuous, so too the sixty are all continuous; that is, they are not completed afterward.
gershom:a24.1: Do the Rabbis hold of dispersed days at all? But they say that she always counts from the second offspring; evidently, according to the Rabbis, the days are always continuous, with no interruption.
gershom:a25.1: Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda: who says she counts from the first offspring; and according to his reasoning one can ask whether they are continuous or dispersed. And since it gives sixty continuous days together, as it says, “just as a day is entirely continuous,” conclude from it that he holds a stringency: the days of impurity of the second count toward the sixty of the first.
gershom:a26.1: Actually, it is the Rabbis; and as for your saying, do they hold of dispersed days at all? What are we dealing with here? Where she gave birth to a male in the eighty [days] of a female, so that the days of purity of the female extend beyond the days of purity of the male, since the days of purity of a male are thirty-three and of a female sixty-six. Lest you say that when the Rabbis said the second voids the first, that applies only where the days of purity of the second extend beyond those of the first; but here, where the days of purity of the first extend beyond those of the second, we say that the law of dispersed days applies, and the days of purity of the first are completed after the days of impurity of the second.
gershom:a27.1: Ultimately: can you really say this? The days of purity of the first are always complete while those of the latter are not yet complete; and where the days of purity of the second extend beyond those of the first, the Rabbis count for the second offspring. And here the days of purity of the second extend well beyond the first. How so? If she conceived a male after the fourteen days of impurity of the female and miscarried at forty-one [days], there remained twenty-five of the female’s sixty-six days of purity, while the male’s days of purity extend for forty days. In such a case the Rabbis hold that the second voids the first. So how do you find dispersed days according to the Rabbis?
gershom:a28.1: Rather, you find it according to the Rabbis, for example, with a woman who gives birth to twins, one female and one male: she bore the female first, and afterward the male lingered in his mother’s womb until the twentieth of the female’s days of purity and was born on day twenty. After the birth of the male there still remained forty-seven days of purity for the female, the twentieth day, the day of the birth, being counted in the total.
gershom:a29.1: And she must take for the male seven days of impurity of birth within those forty-seven days of purity remaining for the female. Here the female’s days of purity extend seven days beyond the male’s days of purity, and one cannot say here that the second voided the first, since the days of purity of the first come later.
gershom:a30.1: And this is what it is saying: one might have thought, where she bore twins, a female first and a male last, after twenty days of purity, say that the impurity of the male’s birth interrupts in the middle and we count for her sixty-six dispersed days: that is, fourteen days after the forty of the male, seven that remained for the female after the male’s days of purity and another seven days completed for her because of the seven days of impurity of the male’s birth that interrupted them. And this is “dispersed” … [the end of the sentence is garbled in the printed text].
gershom:a31.1: One might have thought, dispersed: that they interrupt. This is speaking, for example, where she bore twins, one on the first day and one on the second day, so that the end of the days of impurity of the second enters a day of purity of the first. It asks whether one completes that day of purity of the first that the second rendered impure, or not; and it says: the verse states “day,” that they are all continuous. And conclude from it that Rabbi Yehuda holds a stringency, that they are continuous.
rashi:b1.1: Do they hold of dispersed days? But they count for the second offspring: and since the first is a male, one cannot explain it as it was explained [above], that the days of purity of the first extend beyond the days of purity of the second.
rashi:b1.2: Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda: who counts for the first, and it says that we give her continuous days; evidently she counts from the second.
rashi:b1.3: And conclude from it that he holds a stringency but not a leniency: to extend the days of purity of the first by completing seven others corresponding to the seven days of impurity, and then to assign days of purity to the second as well, which is an excessive leniency.
rashi:b2.1: Six days, etc.: for example, she miscarried after sixty-three [days] of the purity of a female, which are seventy-seven from her birth, when she still had three more days to count; she miscarried, and they became impure. One might have thought that they give her three others corresponding to the three that became impure, so that the six would be dispersed, since here “day” is not written but “days,” which implies even dispersed.
rashi:b2.2: Do they hold of dispersed days? But they count for the second offspring: and the days of this second offspring extend many days beyond the eighty of the first, a female, and you do not find dispersed days. Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda, etc.
rashi:b4.1: MISHNA: The hearing of the voice: “and he heard the voice of adjuration” (Leviticus 5:1).
rashi:b4.2: And the defiling of the Temple: unwittingly; and the utterance of the lips: all of them are written together in the portion of Vayikra concerning the sliding-scale offering, for the verse “Or if a person touches any impure thing,” etc., speaks of the defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods, as explained in the first chapter of Shevuot (7a).
rashi:b5.1: GEMARA: Wealth: a female lamb or a female goat. Poverty: doves or young pigeons. Extreme poverty: a tenth of an ephah.
rashi:b6.1: The hearing of the voice, the utterance of the lips and the defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods: it is explained in Vayikra that they bring in poverty and in extreme poverty.
rashi:b7.1: There are those who bring, etc.: it is explained below.
rashi:b8.1: A woman after childbirth: in wealth, a lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a dove for a sin offering; and in poverty, two doves, that is, a young bird instead of a lamb.
rashi:b8.2: A tenth of an ephah instead of two young birds: that is, one instead of two.
rashi:b9.1: It is incumbent upon me [to bring] a sela: an offering bought for a sela.
rashi:b10.1: (Since throughout the Torah it calls a lamb “in its first year,” by inference a ram is in its second year.)
rashi:b10.2: Since the Merciful One wrote: concerning the guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property, in Vayikra, a ram “in silver shekels,” that is, two sela.
rashi:b10.3:
At a quarter [berova’atayim]: a nest for a quarter-dinar; that is, one brings two young birds in poverty for a quarter-dinar instead of a lamb bought for a sela, which is one-sixteenth of a sela, since a sela is four dinars, and a quarter-dinar is [one of its] sixteen quarters.
In a quarter-dinar there are forty-eight perutot, as we say in the first chapter of Kiddushin (12a): six silver ma’ah are a dinar; a ma’ah is two pundeyon; a pundeyon is two issar; an issar is two mismas; a mismas is two kontrank; and a kontrank is two perutot. That is thirty-two perutot to a ma’ah, and in a ma’ah and a half, which is a quarter-dinar, there are forty-eight perutot. And since you said that extreme poverty, which is a tenth of an ephah, must be one-sixteenth of poverty, it turns out that a tenth of an ephah is three perutot, which is one-sixteenth of forty-eight.
rashi:b14.1: The tanna derives it from a woman after childbirth: he derives poverty from a woman after childbirth, who brings a young bird bought for an eighth of a dinar instead of a lamb bought for a sela, that is, one thirty-second of the lamb, which is twenty-four perutot.
rashi:b14.2: And until now, how much is extreme poverty? One-sixteenth of poverty: granted that you derive from a woman after childbirth that poverty is one thirty-second; but extreme poverty, which is not found with a woman after childbirth, you perforce derive from the lamb and the ram, as we expounded above. For extreme poverty is found only with the hearing of the voice, the utterance of the lips and one who defiles the Temple and its sacred foods, and perforce extreme poverty is derived from their own poverty: just as their poverty is two young birds instead of the lamb, which is one-sixteenth, [so extreme poverty is one-sixteenth] of poverty. And granted that you found poverty elsewhere, as with a woman after childbirth, which is one young bird, an eighth of a dinar, that is, twenty-four perutot; when one brings extreme poverty at one-sixteenth of that, it is a peruta and a half.
rashi:b15.1: The entire matter is derived from a woman after childbirth: even though she has no extreme poverty, it is derived from there: just as we found with her that poverty is one thirty-second of wealth, extreme poverty is also one thirty-second of poverty. The poverty of a woman after childbirth is twenty-four perutot, and extreme poverty is a peruta minus a quarter, which is one thirty-second.
rashi:b17.1: MISHNA: Every sin offering of an individual is a female, that is, a female lamb or a female goat.
rashi:b18.1: Equal with regard to lashes and an offering: if both acted intentionally, both are flogged, as we hold: “When a man or woman shall commit any sin” (Numbers 5:6): the verse equated a woman to a man for all punishments. And if both acted unwittingly, both bring an offering, since for both of them karet is written for the intentional act, as it is written: “And the souls that do them shall be cut off” (Leviticus 18:29), and anything whose intentional violation is punishable by karet requires a sin offering for its unwitting violation.
rashi:b18.2: And with a maidservant, etc.: the woman is flogged and the man brings a guilt offering, as explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b19.1: With all those with whom relations are forbidden, it rendered the initial stage like completion: [this is taught] in tractate Yevamot, in the chapter HaBa al Yevimto (Yevamot 53b).
rashi:b19.2: And with a maidservant, one is liable only for completing the act of intercourse, since “lying of seed” is written concerning her [Leviticus 19:20], [that is, intercourse] that can lead to conception.
rashi:b19.3: And with all those with whom relations are forbidden, he is liable for each and every act of intercourse: but concerning a maidservant they said earlier in our chapter (Keritot 9b) that he brings one offering for many acts of intercourse.
tosafot:b4.1: The defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods: here it counts them as one, and in the first chapter it counts them as two. For there, with regard to karet, they are two, since karet is written for each one; but here, with regard to the offering, both are written with a single karet.
tosafot:b10.1: By inference, a lamb in its first year is a sela: This is difficult, for it says that a sin offering may be worth a danka (in the chapter Eizehu Mekoman, Zevaḥim 48a), and we also say below (Keritot 27a): Why did the Torah not fix a set value for those lacking atonement? Lest lambs become cheaper and they would have no atonement. One can answer: when it says a lamb for a sela, that is the usual practice, to buy it for a sela for the choicest fulfillment of the mitzva, but less is enough. A guilt offering, however, requires “silver shekels” by Torah law, whereas a sin offering has no set value by Torah law, only by rabbinic law. Therefore the mitzva at the outset is a sela, and less is enough down to a danka; one who brings less than a danka is called a transgressor. In any case, if lambs became cheaper and fat ones cost less than a danka, he gains atonement with them. But with guilt offerings, even if they are fat and good, if they cost less than silver shekels because prices fell, he does not gain atonement, since “silver shekels” is written.
tosafot:b10.2: By inference, a lamb in its first year is a sela: that is by rabbinic law, for by Torah law we say everywhere that a sin offering may be worth a danka. And furthermore, Rabbi [our teacher] said: when one brings it at the end of its year, one should bring it for a sela; but from the eighth day on, at the price of an eight-day-old animal, one may bring it even for a danka.
tosafot:b13.1: A tenth of an ephah for a peruta: this does not match the average price mentioned throughout the Talmud, four se’a for a sela, which is an ephah for three dinars; and since six silver ma’ah are a dinar, a tenth of an ephah comes to more than a ma’ah and a half.
gershom:b1.1: [Printed with an editor’s marker: “up to here belongs to 10a.”] And further, come and hear: “six days.” This is speaking, for example, where she bore a female and afterward miscarried during the six days of purity that are beyond the sixty, so that those six days of purity became impure. It asks: one might have thought, regarding those six days, whether we need them continuous with the sixty, so that she loses them because they became impure, or dispersed, so that they are completed after the days of impurity of the second. The verse states “sixty”: just as the sixty are all continuous, since “day” is written of them, so too the six.
gershom:b2.1: Whose is it? If we say the Rabbis, etc.
gershom:b3.1: These bring a sliding-scale offering, etc., and for the defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods: here, with regard to the offering, it counts the defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods as one, but in our first chapter, with regard to karet, it counts them as two, since karet is written for each of them. And here, with regard to sacred foods [an editor’s note suggests reading: with regard to the offering], where only one offering is written for both of them, it counts them as one. Why does it count them as one? For so we say there, in tractate Shevuot: He warned and punished concerning impurity, and imposed an offering concerning impurity, as it is written: “Or if a person touches any impure thing,” with human impurity, etc. Just as when He warned and punished, He punished only for the defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods, as it is written: “She shall touch no hallowed thing,” and He wrote karet for them, so too, the obligation of an offering is only for
gershom:b4.1: the defiling of the Temple and its sacred foods.
gershom:b5.1: A woman after childbirth and a leper bring in poverty and in wealth, for so we find with them. The hearing of the voice, etc., bring even in extreme poverty, that is, a tenth of an ephah, which is written of them. A leper brings in poverty.
gershom:b6.1: For the other baraita is not precise, while that corrected baraita is precise. And even so, my teacher told me: a leper brings in poverty, since when he is poor he brings two young birds instead of two lambs. And the two live, pure birds that even a rich man brings do not come for atonement, but to bring about his purification.
gershom:b7.1: A woman after childbirth brings one instead of one: in her poverty. And what is it? A young bird instead of a lamb; for in her wealth she brings a lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a dove for a sin offering, “and if her means do not suffice for a lamb, then she shall take two doves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering” (Leviticus 12:8). And a leper brings two young birds instead of two lambs that he brings in his wealth, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering, and only one lamb for a guilt offering, since a leper brings a sin offering, a burnt offering and a guilt offering.
gershom:b8.1: The hearing of the voice, etc.: they bring two young birds instead of one female lamb, as is written of them.
gershom:b9.1: Since the Merciful One said ram for a guilt offering: [the guilt offering] for misuse, “according to your valuation in silver shekels, by the shekel of the Sanctuary, for a guilt offering”; and a ram is in its second year; by inference a lamb in its first year is a sela.
gershom:b10.1: And since it is written concerning a woman after childbirth, “she shall bring a lamb in its first year,” which is a sela, and in her poverty she brings nests; and we learned in our previous chapter: nests stood that day at a quarter [berova’atayim], at half a dinar, that is, for two women; so for one woman, a quarter-dinar.
gershom:b11.1: And since the Merciful One had pity on poverty, that it be one-sixteenth of wealth, for the quarter-dinar at which the nest of one woman stood (and every ordinary nest) is one-sixteenth of a sela, as a sela is four dinars; so too the Merciful One had pity on extreme poverty, a tenth of an ephah, that it be one-sixteenth of poverty, of a quarter-dinar.
gershom:b12.1: And how many perutot are in a quarter-dinar? Forty-eight. How so? Six silver ma’ah are a dinar, and a quarter-dinar is a ma’ah and a half; a ma’ah is two pundeyon, so a ma’ah and a half is three pundeyon; a pundeyon is two issar, so a quarter-dinar is six issar; and a peruta is one-eighth of an issar. So there are forty-eight perutot in a quarter-dinar, and one-sixteenth of them is three perutot, since they contain sixteen perutot three times over. So why does it teach: from here you learn that a tenth of an ephah is for a peruta? It is three perutot!
gershom:b13.1: The tanna who teaches a tenth of an ephah for a peruta derives it from a woman after childbirth, who in poverty brings one young bird for a burnt offering instead of a lamb worth a sela. One young bird is half a nest, bought for half a quarter-dinar, that is, one thirty-second of the sela of the lamb; and a whole nest of poverty is one-sixteenth of wealth, as we said.
gershom:b14.1: Rather, he derives it from half a nest, from a young bird instead of a lamb. And extreme poverty, how much is it? One-sixteenth of poverty. A young bird is half a quarter-dinar, and in half a quarter-dinar there are twenty-four perutot; if so, one-sixteenth is a peruta and a half. So why does it teach a tenth of an ephah for a peruta?
gershom:b15.1: Ravina said [the daf’s text reads Rava]: The entire matter, both poverty and extreme poverty, is derived from a woman after childbirth, who brings one young bird [instead of] a lamb; and it does not teach one-sixteenth, as you said, but one thirty-second.
gershom:b16.1: And this is what it says: since the Merciful One had pity on poverty, that it be one thirty-second of a sela, as we said, which is twenty-four perutot, He also had pity on extreme poverty, that it be one thirty-second of poverty, which is one-sixteenth of twelve perutot; and one-sixteenth of twelve perutot is a peruta minus a quarter.
gershom:b17.1: If so: a tenth of an ephah turns out to be a peruta minus a quarter.
gershom:b18.1: Indeed, it is less than a peruta; and the reason it teaches, “from here [you learn that] a tenth of an ephah [is] for a peruta,” is that it is not proper conduct to bring less than a peruta to the Temple.
gershom:b19.1: What is [the difference] between a maidservant and all those with whom relations are forbidden, etc.: not with regard to punishment, for all those with whom relations are forbidden are [punished] either by court-imposed death or by karet, while here it is by lashes.
gershom:b20.1: And with all those with whom relations are forbidden, [both are equal] with regard to the male, since both the male and the female are liable; but the maidservant is liable with regard to the female and not with regard to the male, for there is no liability for the slave.
gershom:b21.1: And he is liable for each and every act of intercourse: which is not so with a maidservant, for he brings one offering for many acts of intercourse.
